title: Review: Dunville’s 1808 Blended Irish Whiskey
summary:
Named after the year the Dunvile’s story began, 1808 is an Irish whiskey blend combining malt, grain, and pot still whiskies. This particular expression was first released in 2021 when the distillery expanded its core range, and is bottled at 40% with no age statement. The post Review: Dunville’s 1808 Blended Irish Whiskey appeared first on Drinkhacker: The Insider's Guide to Good Drinking.
content:
Named after the year the Dunvile’s story began, 1808 is an Irish whiskey blend combining malt, grain, and pot still whiskies. This particular expression was first released in 2021 when the distillery expanded its core range, and is bottled at 40% with no age statement.

Dunville’s 1808 Blended Irish Whiskey Review

The nose is soft and fairly straightforward. Vanilla, green apple, pear, and lemon peel are the main players, with some sweet maltiness sitting underneath, alongside a faint hint of smoke. So far, it’s a pleasant enough dram, but don’t expect layers of complexity.

The palate carries a creamy mouthfeel and is fairly easy-drinking, with lemon, orange, vanilla leading the way. There’s a slight peppery spice and a little char towards the back. The texture is decent, but it does feel a little thin once you start looking for more depth.

The medium-short finish features sweet spice, citrus, and a faint smoky note. Nothing unpleasant, but it disappears fairly quickly.

Overall, this whiskey is fresh, uncomplicated, and a great beginner’s dram. The combination of citrus, orchard fruit, vanilla, and that tiny bit of smoke makes it more interesting than your typical entry-level blend, but there’s certainly not enough weight or complexity here for me to call it an exceptional whiskey – and that’s fine, because it’s not trying to be one.

Where it works really well is as a casual pour or in a cocktail. It’s approachable enough for someone who’s new to whiskey, while still having enough character to stop it being completely forgettable.

Would I choose it over something more serious in the Dunville’s range? No, but again, that’s not what 1808 is trying to accomplish. Either way, my bottle will stay on my shelf and I’m sure the occasion for it will come around. An uncomplicated Irish blend — sometimes it’s exactly what you need!

80 proof.

C / $31

summary:

Green Spot Quails’ Gate is the latest in a trifecta of special Green Spot single pot still Irish whiskeys from Midleton Distillery that crossed the pond back in 2023. First, there’s some back story on…

The post Review: Green Spot Quails’ Gate appeared first on Drinkhacker: The Insider's Guide to Good Drinking.
content:
We’ve covered almost all the Spot whiskeys over the years, but one pesky limited edition has eluded us. Until now. Green Spot Quails’ Gate is the latest in a trifecta of special Green Spot single pot still Irish whiskeys from Midleton Distillery that crossed the pond back in 2023. First, there’s some back story on this series that we may have not yet shared. The unusually named Wine Geese Series in the Spot portfolio celebrates the Irish diaspora, particularly the so-called “wine geese,” Irish families who left Ireland in the early 1700s and established world-class wineries across the globe.

The first release took us to Bordeaux, the second to Napa, and this latest offering hails from a slightly more obscure wine region, British Columbia. Specifically, the winemaker Quails’ Gate which sits in the Okanagan Valley and has a reputation for fantastic Pinot Noir. Like the two other Wine Geese releases before it, this whiskey begins life as classic Green Spot aged in a mix of bourbon and sherry casks before an unspecified finishing in Quails’ Gate Pinot Noir casks. Thoughts follow.

Green Spot Quails’ Gate Review

Like the other two releases in this series, Quails’ Gate manages to offer a nuanced riff on the flagship Spot while still remaining true to the classic pot still whiskey at its core. The nose kicks off with that familiar, funky pot still spice, some barley sugar, and budding notes of banana bread and split vanilla bean. The finishing cask is nicely integrated into the aroma, delivering undertones of raspberry jam and currants that become richer blackberry cobbler as things open in the glass.

The palate showcases early notes of lemon custard and toffee that are balanced and almost buttery in texture. The tannins from the Pinot cask have reined in some of the more traditional Green Spot sweetness, adding a bit of structure and grip along with woody spices and silky notes of black cherry and orange marmalade. The finish is warm and well-spiced with clove and ginger and lingering notes of Linzer cookies and vanilla pudding. Another golden egg, if you will, from the Wine Geese Series.

92 proof.

A- / $100 [BUY IT NOW FROM FROOTBAT]

title: Review: Don Q Reserva and Reserva Especial Rum
summary:
Understanding the various expressions from Puerto Rico’s Don Q can be confusing, with at least four of them called Reserva in some fashion. Reserva 7 Years Old and Gran Reserva Anejo are different than the two rums we look at here today — both new additions to the portfolio. Here’s a look at the latest…

The post Review: Don Q Reserva and Reserva Especial Rum appeared first on Drinkhacker: The Insider's Guide to Good Drinking.
content:
Understanding the various expressions from Puerto Rico’s Don Q can be confusing, with at least four of them called Reserva in some fashion. Reserva 7 Years Old and Gran Reserva Anejo are different than the two rums we look at here today — both new additions to the portfolio.

Here’s a look at the latest duo from Familia Serralles. Aka DonQ.

Both are 80 proof.

Don Q Reserva Rum Review

No age statement, but this blend of rums spends at least five years in former bourbon barrels, so it’s only slightly younger than the Reserva 7 Years Old expression — though it now stands as the youngest Don Q Reserva on the market. This is a quite sweet expression, sweet vanilla and buttercream leading the nose toward increasingly candied territory, with butterscotch dominant. Notes of tannic oak remain in the picture, though, signs that ample maturity runway remains for what amounts to a fairly entry level opening. The palate surprises with less overt sweetness than the nose telegraphs, again moderately tannic and driven by almond, but tempered with bittersweet chocolate and some vague fruit notes, primarily apple. The astringency Jacob mentioned in the 7 Year Old lingers here, though less clearly, perhaps doctored up a bit to wash it away. At least the price is right. B / $21

Don Q Reserva Especial Rum Review

Aged 7 to 10 years in bourbon barrels, placing this as the 3rd most luxe rum in the Reserva lineup. Here a clear tropical character takes hold, with aromas of coconut and pineapple (thankfully) rising from the glass. A more forceful spice, cloves over nutmeg, is also evident, giving the aroma a real tiki quality. At the same time, it’s complemented by a curiously savory note — fish sauce, with its slight saltiness, being the closest analogue I can come up with on short notice.

There’s plenty of fruit on the palate, but soon it shows a more exotic side, fresh pineapple turning toward grilled, coconut toward a toasted character. Layers of raisin and dates come into focus as the initial tropical rush fades, the finish showing a slight florality, before leaning back into darker fruit tones. Maraska cherry hits on the finish, offering a level of depth I didn’t really expect to find here. Twice the price of standard Reserva, and worth it. A- / $40

title: Review: Glenfiddich x Aston Martin Formula One 16 Years Old No. 2 (2026)
summary:
In 2025, Glenfiddich accelerated right into the fray of liquor and racing collabs, announcing a multi-year partnership with the Aston Martin Formula One Team. The initial partnership covered two releases: an ultra-rare 65 year single malt, and a more consumer-conscious 16 year-old, priced for the podium at around $75. For 2026, malt master Brian Kinsman…

The post Review: Glenfiddich x Aston Martin Formula One 16 Years Old No. 2 (2026) appeared first on Drinkhacker: The Insider's Guide to Good Drinking.
content:
In 2025, Glenfiddich accelerated right into the fray of liquor and racing collabs, announcing a multi-year partnership with the Aston Martin Formula One Team. The initial partnership covered two releases: an ultra-rare 65 year single malt, and a more consumer-conscious 16 year-old, priced for the podium at around $75.

For 2026, malt master Brian Kinsman is back with another 16 year single malt, but it’s hardly a rerun of last year’s race. While the inaugural release featured whisky aged across three types of American oak barrels (wine casks, new oak, and second-fill bourbon), the latest model expands to five distinct cask types:

  • first-fill bourbon barrels
  • Port pipes
  • Oloroso sherry casks
  • wine casks (in unspecified varieties)
  • Fino sherry butts, which the brand describes as lending a “final touch”

Like its immediate predecessor, Glenfiddich x Aston Martin Formula One 16 Years Old No. 2 is bottled at 43% ABV. Let’s see how it tastes.

Glenfiddich x Aston Martin Formula One 16 Years Old No. 2 (2026) Review

The nose carries some of that familiar Glenfiddich fruit, but it’s frankly much nuttier than I expected, even with the expanded cask pedigree. (The Port and Fino are doing some heavy lifting!) The most prominent aromas are shoe leather, roasted chestnuts, dehydrated lemon, and dried mission figs. Blackcurrant jam eventually lends some sweetness, which complements the tart dried citrus. Overall, it’s like a series of darker, richer scents were layered atop the classic house profile.

In comparison, early sips are relatively subdued, leading with soft salted caramel before a gradual build of dried orchard fruits. A little citrus zest adds tartness but drops off around (or even just before) the midpalate. That leads to a middle which seems slightly flat in comparison, showcasing honeycomb and preserved fruit syrup but not a whole lot else for complexity. Thankfully, drying spice and black walnut picks up on the back palate, which in combination save the flavor narrative from dullness. Dark chocolate and pipe tobacco guide us through to the finish, which boasts a more dried fruit amidst plenty of lingering oak.

In the end, the spirit leaves a great impression on the nose and solid flavor on the finish. There’s just one thing holding Glenfiddich’s newest blend back: For a brief moment in the middle of the race, its foot comes ever so slightly off the gas.

86 proof.

B+ / $80 [BUY IT NOW FROM FROOTBAT]

summary:
Three guesses where Aspen Vodka hails from! Aspen’s facility is one of the few carbon-negative distilleries in the world and is…

The post Review: Aspen Vodka appeared first on Drinkhacker: The Insider's Guide to Good Drinking.
content:
Three guesses where Aspen Vodka hails from!

Vodka is synonymous with apres ski activities, and true to form, Aspen Distillers makes only one product, a vodka made from non-GMO Colorado wheat and proofed with water from the local Roaring Fork River. Aspen’s facility is one of the few carbon-negative distilleries in the world and is the only North American distillery to receive LEED Platinum v4 certification.

With that, let’s pour a shot and celebrate the arrival of cooler weather.

Aspen Vodka Review

The nose is indistinct, a little grainy, a little muddy, but nothing you can put your finger on. As it gets some air, notes of roasted nuts and dried banana become more prominent, before a layer of earthy forest floor comes into focus, all but taking over.

The palate tells much the same story, but in reverse: First quite dusty and earthy, it blossoms on the tongue to showcase a buttery character, with dusky spices evolving as it sits in the mouth. Light florals, dried like potpourri, along with a wafting incense character, give the finish a heady, Eastern quality — but only slightly. Ultimately, the cereal-heavy elements visible on the initial nosing of the vodka return, leaving the experience slightly doughy.

80 proof.

B / $25 [BUY IT NOW FROM FROOTBAT]

title: Review: Yellowstone Limited Edition Kentucky Straight Bourbon 2026
summary:
Release #11 from Yellowstone’s Limited Edition collection returns to Kentucky straight bourbon (unlike last year’s blend that included Indiana stock), with Port the finishing focus. This edition is a blend of two bourbons, one 7 years old and one 14 years old, finished separately in Ruby and Tawny Port casks before being married and bottled…

The post Review: Yellowstone Limited Edition Kentucky Straight Bourbon 2026 appeared first on Drinkhacker: The Insider's Guide to Good Drinking.
content:
Release #11 from Yellowstone’s Limited Edition collection returns to Kentucky straight bourbon (unlike last year’s blend that included Indiana stock), with Port the finishing focus. This edition is a blend of two bourbons, one 7 years old and one 14 years old, finished separately in Ruby and Tawny Port casks before being married and bottled at 101 proof.

As for the label: “Inspired by the Grand Canyon of the Yellowstone National Park, this year’s expression reflects the contrast between light and shadow that defines one of the park’s most iconic landscapes. The opposing elements guided Beam to finish the bourbons separately – in Ruby Port to evoke the brilliant flare of the canyon’s sunset and Tawny Port to reflect the deep shadow of the valley floor – before bringing them together into a single expression.”

Yellowstone Limited Edition Kentucky Straight Bourbon 2026 Review

Two kinds of Port cask finishing? I expected a sugar bomb from the start, but was surprised to find the nose here to be surprisingly dusky and leaning into earthier notes, extracted fruit lingering under the surface. Time in glass helps to elevate the fruit, but it remains well-tempered by notes of cloves, charred beef, and cherry pits. If anything, the underbelly evokes Tawny Port over Ruby, though both remain indistinct, perhaps overpowered by the quite old bourbon that serves as a base.

The palate tells a similar, yet slightly different story, with fruit more elevated but still short of reaching center stage. Still quite dusky on the tongue, cloves are dominant as a gingerbread character develops, the cherry notes hinted at on the nose finally blooming more fully here. The experience is dense and extracted — Port finally coming further into focus — the finish finally landing on the doughy side. Well-charred like a torched marshmallow, the whiskey goes out not with a whimper but with a bang — complete with lingering notes of gunpowder in the air.

It’s one of the best Yellowstone LE releases to date. Compare to releases from 2016, 2017, 2018, 2019, 2020, 2021, 2022, 2023, 2024, and 2025.

101 proof.

B+ / $99

title: Review: Wines of Post & Beam, 2026 Releases
summary:
This second label of Far Niente launched in 2020 and has quickly proven itself as a more than capable option to reach for when the top shelf option isn’t quite in the budget. We recently received the operation’s core trio of releases for 2026. Thoughts on each bottling follow. 2024 Post & Beam Chardonnay Carneros…

The post Review: Wines of Post & Beam, 2026 Releases appeared first on Drinkhacker: The Insider's Guide to Good Drinking.
content:
This second label of Far Niente launched in 2020 and has quickly proven itself as a more than capable option to reach for when the top shelf option isn’t quite in the budget. We recently received the operation’s core trio of releases for 2026. Thoughts on each bottling follow.

2024 Post & Beam Chardonnay Carneros – A classically oaked California chardonnay, albeit one with ample restraint. Initially a bit doughy and chewy, layers of lemon curd give way to a more patisserie vibe, with almond croissants and pistachio cream lively on the midpalate. The wine’s a bit tight on the finish, with a slight metallic tang, but this acidity does provide a certain cleansing quality, though it can strike a slightly harsh note at times. B+ / $35

2024 Post & Beam Pinot Noir Sonoma Coast – Quite a bit lighter and quite a bit brighter than the typical Sonoma Coast pinot noir bottling, here we discover a delightful by-the-glass offering that offers moderated fruit — cherry, black raspberry, then some rhubarb — tempered by a shovelful of turned earth, a pinch of graphite, and just a hint of chewy, perhaps canned, green bean. The slight funkiness doesn’t overly mar what is otherwise a fairly bright, light-handed, and versatile experience, one which pairs genially with a wide range of foods — or nothing at all. A- / $40

2023 Post & Beam Cabernet Sauvignon Napa Valley – Surprisingly restrained, what could have been a workaday cab reveals itself to offer tannic restraint, alongside a significant gingerbread character and notes of (very) dark chocolate and dried herbs, with sage surprisingly prominent. A husky clove-heavy character infuses a finish that lets up as it sees some cab trademark currant notes finally coming into the fore, returning to cocoa notes for a gently dessert-adjacent denouement. B+ / $40

title: Review: Johnnie Walker Blue Label Festive Blend
summary:
It’s been two years since we last reviewed a Blue Label special edition, having greatly enjoyed the Ice Chalet offering from 2024. This year, Johnnie Walker has dropped something entirely new, officially known on the label as “Festive Blend” but unofficially as “Indian Festive Blend.” The festival in question is ostensibly Diwali, the late fall…

The post Review: Johnnie Walker Blue Label Festive Blend appeared first on Drinkhacker: The Insider's Guide to Good Drinking.
content:
It’s been two years since we last reviewed a Blue Label special edition, having greatly enjoyed the Ice Chalet offering from 2024. This year, Johnnie Walker has dropped something entirely new, officially known on the label as “Festive Blend” but unofficially as “Indian Festive Blend.”

The festival in question is ostensibly Diwali, the late fall festival of lights celebrated in Hindu culture. Johnnie Walker master blender Dr. Emma Walker chose tasks that resonated with this event: “I was captivated by the artistry of Indian cuisine, the way chefs balance bold spice with harmony, elegance and depth,” she says. “That sense of balance became my inspiration for this special Blue Label blend. By layering aromatic notes of cardamom, clove and cinnamon with smooth sweetness and our signature depth of flavor, we’ve created a whisky that complements the richness of India’s festive table while remaining unmistakably Johnnie Walker Blue Label.”

The bottle was designed in collaboration with Indian couturier Rahul Mishra, who worked with Johnnie Walker on another Indian-themed release in 2025 for Paris Fashion Week.

We were fortunate to receive a bottle for review. Our thoughts follow.

Johnnie Walker Blue Label Festive Blend Review

Just nosing this whisky reveals what an all-star Emma Walker is at cask selection, particularly given she has about 10 million of them to work with at any one time. The nose here truly evokes an Indian celebration, with cardamom and cinnamon immediately present. It’s quite heady, with a brown butter sensibility that tempers any risk of the spice notes running away from you, developing into a deeper and more soulful aroma that releases notes of gently tanned leather and graphite, as the spice turns more toward clove. Some chocolate notes, bittersweet to dark, come along soon enough.

The palate is an utter delight. Lightly sweet with honey and more of a milk chocolate note, it’s a perfect foil to the increasingly aromatic nose, which could threaten to overwhelm if not for the subduing qualities that are part and parcel of the palate. Notes of chocolate-covered orange, graham crackers, and orange blossom honey all sweeten up the experience, though those intensely spicy elements evident on the nose remain well-integrated in the body. The finish sees some lingering cereal notes, offering a breakfasty conclusion to the ride, though maybe just a little too grain-forward given what’s come before.

This is one of those whiskies that is difficult to put down once you pop the cork, its enchanting depth of flavor pulling you in on the nose, then holding fast on the tongue. Whether you’re celebrating Diwali or not — or even know what it is — it’s an absolute star, unique without being bizarre, engaging through and through.

81.6 proof.

A / $220 [BUY IT NOW FROM FROOTBAT]

title: Review: Jack Daniel’s Single Barrel Special Release 2026 – Coy Hill Rye
summary:

The tiny distillery in Lynchburg, Tennessee has returned to this hallowed rickhouse for a third time, only this time with a twist, turning out a rye whiskey instead of a bourbon (or a classic Tennessee whiskey, if you please). Coy Hill Rye follows the theme…

The post Review: Jack Daniel’s Single Barrel Special Release 2026 – Coy Hill Rye appeared first on Drinkhacker: The Insider's Guide to Good Drinking.
content:
Jack Daniel’s just can’t leave the warehouse at Coy Hill alone. The tiny distillery in Lynchburg, Tennessee has returned to this hallowed rickhouse for a third time, only this time with a twist, turning out a rye whiskey instead of a bourbon (or a classic Tennessee whiskey, if you please).

Coy Hill Rye follows the theme of the prior Coy Hill releases with its upper floor aging and the resulting hazmat sensibility — though it’s probably worth noting that at a mere 66.55% abv (133.1 proof), my sample has the lowest proof level of the three Coy Hill releases I’ve tasted to date. However, proofs vary widely by barrel, ranging from 128.7 to 148.5.

In the bottle is from the classic JD rye recipe: 70% rye, 18% corn, and 12% malted barley. JD’s charcoal mellowing is minimal with its rye, going through just 3 feet of charcoal before entering the barrel, a process that takes only a few minutes. Distilled in 2016, about 300 barrels of 10 year old (or almost 10 year old) whiskeys were pulled for this release.

Let’s give it a try.

Jack Daniel’s Single Barrel Special Release 2026 – Coy Hill Rye Review

Old rye can often be bruising with its intense, peppery spice, and at over 66% abv that impact can be far more powerful. A mix of fresh, herb-heavy greenery kicks things off, and a charry, toasted marshmallow character lands right behind it. From there, the whiskey takes on a sweeter bent, a combination of gingerbread and butterscotch, both coming across as slightly burnt but in a good way. Further time in glass evokes notes of brown banana and pastry crust, rather more bourbon-like in tone.

The palate doesn’t immediately come across as overtly hot, the notes of banana and butterscotch making for a quite immersive, almost decadent attack. The aggressively green spices have blown off at this point, leaving behind a heavy punch of baking spice, with more cinnamon and ginger than clove in the mix. The heady nose, with its evolving incense notes, amplifies the spice box character beautifully, the finish eventually settling into lingering notes of tobacco, followed by a ring of sweetened licorice. And here’s the crazy thing: I never once thought this needed to be tempered with water. (I ultimately tried dosing it with a splash, but I stand by my earlier decision.)

Good rye is easy to come by. Great rye is tough to find. Sadly, my expectation is that this one will also be nearly impossible to get — but you might as well try.

133.1 proof as reviewed.

A / $90 [BUY IT NOW FROM FROOTBAT]

summary:

Recently we received one of its offerings, a trilogy of white wines from various locales in France (Burgundy, Chateauneuf-du-Pape, and Alsace) called The…

The post Review: The WSJ Iconic Wines of France Trio 2026 appeared first on Drinkhacker: The Insider's Guide to Good Drinking.
content:
Years ago the Wall Street Journal had a prominent if slightly bizarre wine review section. While that has faded away, the news operation still markets wine for purchase through a club of sorts. Recently we received one of its offerings, a trilogy of white wines from various locales in France (Burgundy, Chateauneuf-du-Pape, and Alsace) called The WSJ Wine Iconic Whites of France Trio.

The full set is available for a limited time. We’re also including pricing for the bottles if you were to source them individually.

2023 Château Sixtine Châteauneuf-du-Pape Blanc – Quite luscious with overtones of peach cobbler and apricots in syrup, undercut with gentle salinity and minerality. It’s a soothing wine with lingering sweetness, while notes of orchard blossoms perk up the aromatics as the finish lingers. Touches of vanilla arrive late, applied with the lightest of hands. A / $67

2023 M. Dutron Pouilly-Fuissé Vieilles Vignes – A classic expression of chardonnay from Burgundy, bright with lemon but touched with green apple and some white peach notes. A classic green table grape character evolves on the brightly acidic midpalate, a gentle salinity offering a cleansing and exceptionally bright finish. Hints of fresh linen take you out of what is, from start to finish, an iconically Burgundian journey. A / $51

2023 Edouard Leiber Riesling Grand Cru Pfingstberg – Quite tart, this wine is effusive with up-front green apple and pear notes, heavy with lime and lemon, but time in glass makes room for a significant note of honey, particularly on the heavy nose. The wine settles down with a little warmth and time in glass,  the honey-lemon finish ultimately evoking a glass of chilled tea. B+ / $50

$140 for the set [BUY IT NOW FROM WSJ WINE]

title: Review: Old Forester The 117 Series – Triple Char Bourbon
summary:
This newest expression in Old Forester’s 117 Series almost slipped by us. Crafted entirely at Old Forester’s Main Street Louisville location, it’s a boldly experimental offering called Triple Char. As the name suggests, it’s made using barrels charred for three times the usual length of time than Old Forester normally uses. OldFo typically uses a…

The post Review: Old Forester The 117 Series – Triple Char Bourbon appeared first on Drinkhacker: The Insider's Guide to Good Drinking.
content:
This newest expression in Old Forester’s 117 Series almost slipped by us. Crafted entirely at Old Forester’s Main Street Louisville location, it’s a boldly experimental offering called Triple Char. As the name suggests, it’s made using barrels charred for three times the usual length of time than Old Forester normally uses. OldFo typically uses a Level 4 char — about 55 seconds of char time, which means the barrels used here spend nearly 3 minutes exposed to open flame. This equates to roughly a char Level 7, something we’ve seen in a couple of other experimental offerings.

Let’s give it a spin.

Old Forester The 117 Series – Triple Char Bourbon Review

Surprisingly, the nose of this ambitious spirit evokes far more than charred wood. Notes of mint and cherry are quite prominent, backed with a heavy chocolate and ground coffee character. There’s plenty of that charry, almost smoky oak in attendance, but the surfeit of additional flavors in the mix helps the whiskey exude aromatic complexity.

The palate keeps all of this rolling right along. Big, burnt caramel flavors lead to layers of coconut and banana, then baked green apples. Quite nutty as it develops, the whiskey quickly navigates its way into a vein of baking spice, big with cloves and a punch of toasted, ground ginger. Above all this bourbon is intense. That may be the amplifying effect of the ultra-torched oak staves — or the oak in combination with the high abv — but the whole affair comes to a head on the in-your-face finish, which is tart and tannic in equal proportions. Time in glass turns things into a real vanilla bomb, though greener herbs, namely bay leaf, always linger in the background.

These ultra-charred releases are always worth investigating to help understand the power of heavily charred oak. If you find it at the distillery, it’s a sample worth picking up.

115 proof.

A- / $65 (375ml)

title: Review: Dunville’s 1808 Blended Irish Whiskey
summary:
Named after the year the Dunvile’s story began, 1808 is an Irish whiskey blend combining malt, grain, and pot still whiskies. This particular expression was first released in 2021 when the distillery expanded its core range, and is bottled at 40% with no age statement. Dunville’s 1808 Blended Irish Whiskey Review The nose is soft…

The post Review: Dunville’s 1808 Blended Irish Whiskey appeared first on Drinkhacker: The Insider's Guide to Good Drinking.
content:
Named after the year the Dunvile’s story began, 1808 is an Irish whiskey blend combining malt, grain, and pot still whiskies. This particular expression was first released in 2021 when the distillery expanded its core range, and is bottled at 40% with no age statement.

Dunville’s 1808 Blended Irish Whiskey Review

The nose is soft and fairly straightforward. Vanilla, green apple, pear, and lemon peel are the main players, with some sweet maltiness sitting underneath, alongside a faint hint of smoke. So far, it’s a pleasant enough dram, but don’t expect layers of complexity.

The palate carries a creamy mouthfeel and is fairly easy-drinking, with lemon, orange, vanilla leading the way. There’s a slight peppery spice and a little char towards the back. The texture is decent, but it does feel a little thin once you start looking for more depth.

The medium-short finish features sweet spice, citrus, and a faint smoky note. Nothing unpleasant, but it disappears fairly quickly.

Overall, this whiskey is fresh, uncomplicated, and a great beginner’s dram. The combination of citrus, orchard fruit, vanilla, and that tiny bit of smoke makes it more interesting than your typical entry-level blend, but there’s certainly not enough weight or complexity here for me to call it an exceptional whiskey – and that’s fine, because it’s not trying to be one.

Where it works really well is as a casual pour or in a cocktail. It’s approachable enough for someone who’s new to whiskey, while still having enough character to stop it being completely forgettable.

Would I choose it over something more serious in the Dunville’s range? No, but again, that’s not what 1808 is trying to accomplish. Either way, my bottle will stay on my shelf and I’m sure the occasion for it will come around. An uncomplicated Irish blend — sometimes it’s exactly what you need!

80 proof.

C / $31

title: Review: Green Spot Quails’ Gate
summary:
We’ve covered almost all the Spot whiskeys over the years, but one pesky limited edition has eluded us. Until now. Green Spot Quails’ Gate is the latest in a trifecta of special Green Spot single pot still Irish whiskeys from Midleton Distillery that crossed the pond back in 2023. First, there’s some back story on…

The post Review: Green Spot Quails’ Gate appeared first on Drinkhacker: The Insider's Guide to Good Drinking.
content:
We’ve covered almost all the Spot whiskeys over the years, but one pesky limited edition has eluded us. Until now. Green Spot Quails’ Gate is the latest in a trifecta of special Green Spot single pot still Irish whiskeys from Midleton Distillery that crossed the pond back in 2023. First, there’s some back story on this series that we may have not yet shared. The unusually named Wine Geese Series in the Spot portfolio celebrates the Irish diaspora, particularly the so-called “wine geese,” Irish families who left Ireland in the early 1700s and established world-class wineries across the globe.

The first release took us to Bordeaux, the second to Napa, and this latest offering hails from a slightly more obscure wine region, British Columbia. Specifically, the winemaker Quails’ Gate which sits in the Okanagan Valley and has a reputation for fantastic Pinot Noir. Like the two other Wine Geese releases before it, this whiskey begins life as classic Green Spot aged in a mix of bourbon and sherry casks before an unspecified finishing in Quails’ Gate Pinot Noir casks. Thoughts follow.

Green Spot Quails’ Gate Review

Like the other two releases in this series, Quails’ Gate manages to offer a nuanced riff on the flagship Spot while still remaining true to the classic pot still whiskey at its core. The nose kicks off with that familiar, funky pot still spice, some barley sugar, and budding notes of banana bread and split vanilla bean. The finishing cask is nicely integrated into the aroma, delivering undertones of raspberry jam and currants that become richer blackberry cobbler as things open in the glass.

The palate showcases early notes of lemon custard and toffee that are balanced and almost buttery in texture. The tannins from the Pinot cask have reined in some of the more traditional Green Spot sweetness, adding a bit of structure and grip along with woody spices and silky notes of black cherry and orange marmalade. The finish is warm and well-spiced with clove and ginger and lingering notes of Linzer cookies and vanilla pudding. Another golden egg, if you will, from the Wine Geese Series.

92 proof.

A- / $100 [BUY IT NOW FROM FROOTBAT]

title: Review: Don Q Reserva and Reserva Especial Rum
summary:
Understanding the various expressions from Puerto Rico’s Don Q can be confusing, with at least four of them called Reserva in some fashion. Reserva 7 Years Old and Gran Reserva Anejo are different than the two rums we look at here today — both new additions to the portfolio. Here’s a look at the latest…

The post Review: Don Q Reserva and Reserva Especial Rum appeared first on Drinkhacker: The Insider's Guide to Good Drinking.
content:
Understanding the various expressions from Puerto Rico’s Don Q can be confusing, with at least four of them called Reserva in some fashion. Reserva 7 Years Old and Gran Reserva Anejo are different than the two rums we look at here today — both new additions to the portfolio.

Here’s a look at the latest duo from Familia Serralles. Aka DonQ.

Both are 80 proof.

Don Q Reserva Rum Review

No age statement, but this blend of rums spends at least five years in former bourbon barrels, so it’s only slightly younger than the Reserva 7 Years Old expression — though it now stands as the youngest Don Q Reserva on the market. This is a quite sweet expression, sweet vanilla and buttercream leading the nose toward increasingly candied territory, with butterscotch dominant. Notes of tannic oak remain in the picture, though, signs that ample maturity runway remains for what amounts to a fairly entry level opening. The palate surprises with less overt sweetness than the nose telegraphs, again moderately tannic and driven by almond, but tempered with bittersweet chocolate and some vague fruit notes, primarily apple. The astringency Jacob mentioned in the 7 Year Old lingers here, though less clearly, perhaps doctored up a bit to wash it away. At least the price is right. B / $21

Don Q Reserva Especial Rum Review

Aged 7 to 10 years in bourbon barrels, placing this as the 3rd most luxe rum in the Reserva lineup. Here a clear tropical character takes hold, with aromas of coconut and pineapple (thankfully) rising from the glass. A more forceful spice, cloves over nutmeg, is also evident, giving the aroma a real tiki quality. At the same time, it’s complemented by a curiously savory note — fish sauce, with its slight saltiness, being the closest analogue I can come up with on short notice.

There’s plenty of fruit on the palate, but soon it shows a more exotic side, fresh pineapple turning toward grilled, coconut toward a toasted character. Layers of raisin and dates come into focus as the initial tropical rush fades, the finish showing a slight florality, before leaning back into darker fruit tones. Maraska cherry hits on the finish, offering a level of depth I didn’t really expect to find here. Twice the price of standard Reserva, and worth it. A- / $40

summary:

content:
ADVERTISEMENT

Casino resorts offer more than gambling, and some have become destinations for whisky enthusiasts. While online casinos come up with offers like 100 free spins no deposit, land-based casinos have been able to bring people in by providing something other than gambling, such as bars with a collection of whiskies. Ranging from the unusual kinds of Scotch whisky to a particular bottling line, these places serve those looking for something more than just the usual cocktail menu. Here is a review of six whisky bars in casinos located in Las Vegas and Macau.

Which Casino Whisky Bars Have the Most Impressive Collections?

Every venue below had to pass the same three checks before it earned a place on the list. Bottle counts differ from source to source, so figures are given as reported:

  • Named sources. The collection is described by a publication or an official venue page, mostly dated between 2018 and 2026.
  • Depth or character. The list shows old or limited bottles, private casks, or an unusual focus on one distillery.
  • Specific bottles. Where possible, a source names real ages, vintages, or labels.

Four of the bars are in Las Vegas, and two are in Macau, a sign that serious whisky lists have spread beyond the Strip. Menus change often, so treat the table below as a starting point.

Bar Resort and city Reported collection Bottles named by sources
Emeril’s Delmonico Steakhouse The Venetian, Las Vegas Around 800 labelS Ladyburn 1973, Glen Grant 1958
Scotch 80 Prime Palms, Las Vegas Around 500 bottles Macallan Fine and Rare, back to 1937
Tower Suites Bar Wynn, Las Vegas 100+ options Macallan 25, Hibiki 21
Whiskey Down MGM Grand, Las Vegas 50+ to about 300 Macallan 1946
Pony & Plume Capella, Galaxy Macau Over 650 varieties None named
The Macallan Whisky Bar & Lounge Galaxy Macau Over 400 malts None named

 

The table shows how far the six collections differ in size and in the way sources describe them. The details behind each row follow, bar by bar, so you can see where each claim comes from.

Emeril’s Delmonico Steakhouse, The Venetian, Las Vegas

Delmonico is a steakhouse, yet its whisky list is the reason whisky travelers know it. Visit Las Vegas describes old Scotch as “many over 30 years” and private single casks. In a 2020 guide by Whisky Advocate, 34-year-old Duncan Taylor Ladyburn 1973, 50-year-old Glen Grant 1958, and Pappy Van Winkle 23 Year Old are mentioned. You may want to confirm if they are still available before you consider planning around them.

Scotch 80 Prime, Palms Casino Resort, Las Vegas

Scotch 80 Prime built its reputation on one producer. Visit Las Vegas describes a Macallan Fine and Rare vintage collection of nearly three dozen bottles. In a 2018 interview, the venue’s scotch master called its 33 Macallan marques, dating back to 1937, the largest such collection available for consumption. That is the venue’s own claim. The restaurant still appears on Las Vegas Advisor, but confirm that it is open and that the whisky list is current.

Tower Suites Bar, Wynn Las Vegas

This lobby bar sits in the Wynn Tower Suites, away from the casino noise. A 2023 Whisky Advocate guide counted more than 100 options and named Macallan 25 Year Old, Hibiki 21 Year Old, Michter’s 20 Year Old, and Pappy Van Winkle 15 and 23 Year Old. The list is smaller than Delmonico’s, but its named bottles lean toward aged and hard-to-find releases.

Whiskey Down, MGM Grand, Las Vegas

Whiskey Down stands out for its rare bottlings. Visit Las Vegas mentions old Macallans, Gordon & MacPhail bottlings, and Kavalan, while a 2020 Whisky Advocate guide names Macallan 1946 and 1997, bottled for the bar at 46% ABV. A 2025 source lists more than 50 choices, while a 2020 report counted about 300 whiskies, so the exact size of the collection is hard to pin down.

Pony & Plume, Capella at Galaxy Macau, Macau

In March 2026, the South China Morning Post reported that this whisky bar holds over 650 varieties of rare and unique whiskies. The article names no individual bottles, so the claim of rarity rests on that report.

The Macallan Whisky Bar & Lounge, Galaxy Macau

Galaxy Macau’s own page describes more than 400 malt whiskies and the rarest selections from The Macallan. No specific bottles are named, so ask what is available on the night you visit.

What Makes a Casino Whisky Collection Stand Out?

A serious collection goes beyond an ordinary menu in several ways, and the venues above show each of them at work:

  • Vintage depth. Old expressions of one distillery, such as the Macallan marques at Scotch 80 Prime, matter more than one bottle of each label.
  • Private casks. Bottlings made for a single venue, as at Delmonico and Whiskey Down, cannot be found elsewhere.
  • Named bottles. A list that states ages and vintages, like the Wynn list, can be checked in advance.
  • Guidance. Annotated lists, such as the distillery map at Delmonico, help guests choose.

Size alone is not the point: 100 carefully chosen aged bottles can be more interesting than 800 standard labels. A promise of a “rare selection” means little without names: a list that states bottles and vintages lets you check before you go and decide whether the trip is worth it.

How to Choose a Casino Whisky Bar for a Special Tasting?

A little planning goes a long way, since rare pours sell out and menus change without notice. Work through this checklist before you go:

  • Current list. Check whether the whisky list is published online and whether your target bottles are marked as available.
  • Tasting options. Ask about flights or small pours, which let you try an old bottle without buying a full measure.
  • Reservation. Book a table when the venue takes bookings, especially at steakhouse-based bars such as Scotch 80 Prime.
  • Prices. Ask the cost of rare pours before you sit down, because named sources rarely publish them.
  • Opening hours. Confirm the schedule, as the 2020 guide described Whiskey Down as open around the clock.

The sources of this guide were written between 2018 and 2026, so there may be differences in the available bottles and information since then. In terms of selecting between bars, you should choose a bar that has a comprehensive list and guides for tastings.

title: Review: Glenfiddich x Aston Martin Formula One 16 Years Old No. 2 (2026)
summary:
In 2025, Glenfiddich accelerated right into the fray of liquor and racing collabs, announcing a multi-year partnership with the Aston Martin Formula One Team. The initial partnership covered two releases: an ultra-rare 65 year single malt, and a more consumer-conscious 16 year-old, priced for the podium at around $75. For 2026, malt master Brian Kinsman…

The post Review: Glenfiddich x Aston Martin Formula One 16 Years Old No. 2 (2026) appeared first on Drinkhacker: The Insider's Guide to Good Drinking.
content:
In 2025, Glenfiddich accelerated right into the fray of liquor and racing collabs, announcing a multi-year partnership with the Aston Martin Formula One Team. The initial partnership covered two releases: an ultra-rare 65 year single malt, and a more consumer-conscious 16 year-old, priced for the podium at around $75.

For 2026, malt master Brian Kinsman is back with another 16 year single malt, but it’s hardly a rerun of last year’s race. While the inaugural release featured whisky aged across three types of American oak barrels (wine casks, new oak, and second-fill bourbon), the latest model expands to five distinct cask types:

  • first-fill bourbon barrels
  • Port pipes
  • Oloroso sherry casks
  • wine casks (in unspecified varieties)
  • Fino sherry butts, which the brand describes as lending a “final touch”

Like its immediate predecessor, Glenfiddich x Aston Martin Formula One 16 Years Old No. 2 is bottled at 43% ABV. Let’s see how it tastes.

Glenfiddich x Aston Martin Formula One 16 Years Old No. 2 (2026) Review

The nose carries some of that familiar Glenfiddich fruit, but it’s frankly much nuttier than I expected, even with the expanded cask pedigree. (The Port and Fino are doing some heavy lifting!) The most prominent aromas are shoe leather, roasted chestnuts, dehydrated lemon, and dried mission figs. Blackcurrant jam eventually lends some sweetness, which complements the tart dried citrus. Overall, it’s like a series of darker, richer scents were layered atop the classic house profile.

In comparison, early sips are relatively subdued, leading with soft salted caramel before a gradual build of dried orchard fruits. A little citrus zest adds tartness but drops off around (or even just before) the midpalate. That leads to a middle which seems slightly flat in comparison, showcasing honeycomb and preserved fruit syrup but not a whole lot else for complexity. Thankfully, drying spice and black walnut picks up on the back palate, which in combination save the flavor narrative from dullness. Dark chocolate and pipe tobacco guide us through to the finish, which boasts a more dried fruit amidst plenty of lingering oak.

In the end, the spirit leaves a great impression on the nose and solid flavor on the finish. There’s just one thing holding Glenfiddich’s newest blend back: For a brief moment in the middle of the race, its foot comes ever so slightly off the gas.

86 proof.

B+ / $80 [BUY IT NOW FROM FROOTBAT]

The post Review: Aspen Vodka appeared first on Drinkhacker: The Insider's Guide to Good Drinking.
content:
Three guesses where Aspen Vodka hails from!

Vodka is synonymous with apres ski activities, and true to form, Aspen Distillers makes only one product, a vodka made from non-GMO Colorado wheat and proofed with water from the local Roaring Fork River. Aspen’s facility is one of the few carbon-negative distilleries in the world and is the only North American distillery to receive LEED Platinum v4 certification.

With that, let’s pour a shot and celebrate the arrival of cooler weather.

Aspen Vodka Review

The nose is indistinct, a little grainy, a little muddy, but nothing you can put your finger on. As it gets some air, notes of roasted nuts and dried banana become more prominent, before a layer of earthy forest floor comes into focus, all but taking over.

The palate tells much the same story, but in reverse: First quite dusty and earthy, it blossoms on the tongue to showcase a buttery character, with dusky spices evolving as it sits in the mouth. Light florals, dried like potpourri, along with a wafting incense character, give the finish a heady, Eastern quality — but only slightly. Ultimately, the cereal-heavy elements visible on the initial nosing of the vodka return, leaving the experience slightly doughy.

80 proof.

B / $25 [BUY IT NOW FROM FROOTBAT]

title: Review: Yellowstone Limited Edition Kentucky Straight Bourbon 2026
summary:
Release #11 from Yellowstone’s Limited Edition collection returns to Kentucky straight bourbon (unlike last year’s blend that included Indiana stock), with Port the finishing focus. This edition is a blend of two bourbons, one 7 years old and one 14 years old, finished separately in Ruby and Tawny Port casks before being married and bottled…

The post Review: Yellowstone Limited Edition Kentucky Straight Bourbon 2026 appeared first on Drinkhacker: The Insider's Guide to Good Drinking.
content:
Release #11 from Yellowstone’s Limited Edition collection returns to Kentucky straight bourbon (unlike last year’s blend that included Indiana stock), with Port the finishing focus. This edition is a blend of two bourbons, one 7 years old and one 14 years old, finished separately in Ruby and Tawny Port casks before being married and bottled at 101 proof.

As for the label: “Inspired by the Grand Canyon of the Yellowstone National Park, this year’s expression reflects the contrast between light and shadow that defines one of the park’s most iconic landscapes. The opposing elements guided Beam to finish the bourbons separately – in Ruby Port to evoke the brilliant flare of the canyon’s sunset and Tawny Port to reflect the deep shadow of the valley floor – before bringing them together into a single expression.”

Yellowstone Limited Edition Kentucky Straight Bourbon 2026 Review

Two kinds of Port cask finishing? I expected a sugar bomb from the start, but was surprised to find the nose here to be surprisingly dusky and leaning into earthier notes, extracted fruit lingering under the surface. Time in glass helps to elevate the fruit, but it remains well-tempered by notes of cloves, charred beef, and cherry pits. If anything, the underbelly evokes Tawny Port over Ruby, though both remain indistinct, perhaps overpowered by the quite old bourbon that serves as a base.

The palate tells a similar, yet slightly different story, with fruit more elevated but still short of reaching center stage. Still quite dusky on the tongue, cloves are dominant as a gingerbread character develops, the cherry notes hinted at on the nose finally blooming more fully here. The experience is dense and extracted — Port finally coming further into focus — the finish finally landing on the doughy side. Well-charred like a torched marshmallow, the whiskey goes out not with a whimper but with a bang — complete with lingering notes of gunpowder in the air.

It’s one of the best Yellowstone LE releases to date. Compare to releases from 2016, 2017, 2018, 2019, 2020, 2021, 2022, 2023, 2024, and 2025.

101 proof.

B+ / $99

summary:

We recently received the operation’s core trio of releases for 2026. Thoughts on each bottling follow. 2024 Post & Beam Chardonnay Carneros…

The post Review: Wines of Post & Beam, 2026 Releases appeared first on Drinkhacker: The Insider's Guide to Good Drinking.
content:
This second label of Far Niente launched in 2020 and has quickly proven itself as a more than capable option to reach for when the top shelf option isn’t quite in the budget. We recently received the operation’s core trio of releases for 2026. Thoughts on each bottling follow.

2024 Post & Beam Chardonnay Carneros – A classically oaked California chardonnay, albeit one with ample restraint. Initially a bit doughy and chewy, layers of lemon curd give way to a more patisserie vibe, with almond croissants and pistachio cream lively on the midpalate. The wine’s a bit tight on the finish, with a slight metallic tang, but this acidity does provide a certain cleansing quality, though it can strike a slightly harsh note at times. B+ / $35

2024 Post & Beam Pinot Noir Sonoma Coast – Quite a bit lighter and quite a bit brighter than the typical Sonoma Coast pinot noir bottling, here we discover a delightful by-the-glass offering that offers moderated fruit — cherry, black raspberry, then some rhubarb — tempered by a shovelful of turned earth, a pinch of graphite, and just a hint of chewy, perhaps canned, green bean. The slight funkiness doesn’t overly mar what is otherwise a fairly bright, light-handed, and versatile experience, one which pairs genially with a wide range of foods — or nothing at all. A- / $40

2023 Post & Beam Cabernet Sauvignon Napa Valley – Surprisingly restrained, what could have been a workaday cab reveals itself to offer tannic restraint, alongside a significant gingerbread character and notes of (very) dark chocolate and dried herbs, with sage surprisingly prominent. A husky clove-heavy character infuses a finish that lets up as it sees some cab trademark currant notes finally coming into the fore, returning to cocoa notes for a gently dessert-adjacent denouement. B+ / $40

title: Review: Johnnie Walker Blue Label Festive Blend
summary:
It’s been two years since we last reviewed a Blue Label special edition, having greatly enjoyed the Ice Chalet offering from 2024. This year, Johnnie Walker has dropped something entirely new, officially known on the label as “Festive Blend” but unofficially as “Indian Festive Blend.” The festival in question is ostensibly Diwali, the late fall…

The post Review: Johnnie Walker Blue Label Festive Blend appeared first on Drinkhacker: The Insider's Guide to Good Drinking.
content:
It’s been two years since we last reviewed a Blue Label special edition, having greatly enjoyed the Ice Chalet offering from 2024. This year, Johnnie Walker has dropped something entirely new, officially known on the label as “Festive Blend” but unofficially as “Indian Festive Blend.”

The festival in question is ostensibly Diwali, the late fall festival of lights celebrated in Hindu culture. Johnnie Walker master blender Dr. Emma Walker chose tasks that resonated with this event: “I was captivated by the artistry of Indian cuisine, the way chefs balance bold spice with harmony, elegance and depth,” she says. “That sense of balance became my inspiration for this special Blue Label blend. By layering aromatic notes of cardamom, clove and cinnamon with smooth sweetness and our signature depth of flavor, we’ve created a whisky that complements the richness of India’s festive table while remaining unmistakably Johnnie Walker Blue Label.”

The bottle was designed in collaboration with Indian couturier Rahul Mishra, who worked with Johnnie Walker on another Indian-themed release in 2025 for Paris Fashion Week.

We were fortunate to receive a bottle for review. Our thoughts follow.

Johnnie Walker Blue Label Festive Blend Review

Just nosing this whisky reveals what an all-star Emma Walker is at cask selection, particularly given she has about 10 million of them to work with at any one time. The nose here truly evokes an Indian celebration, with cardamom and cinnamon immediately present. It’s quite heady, with a brown butter sensibility that tempers any risk of the spice notes running away from you, developing into a deeper and more soulful aroma that releases notes of gently tanned leather and graphite, as the spice turns more toward clove. Some chocolate notes, bittersweet to dark, come along soon enough.

The palate is an utter delight. Lightly sweet with honey and more of a milk chocolate note, it’s a perfect foil to the increasingly aromatic nose, which could threaten to overwhelm if not for the subduing qualities that are part and parcel of the palate. Notes of chocolate-covered orange, graham crackers, and orange blossom honey all sweeten up the experience, though those intensely spicy elements evident on the nose remain well-integrated in the body. The finish sees some lingering cereal notes, offering a breakfasty conclusion to the ride, though maybe just a little too grain-forward given what’s come before.

This is one of those whiskies that is difficult to put down once you pop the cork, its enchanting depth of flavor pulling you in on the nose, then holding fast on the tongue. Whether you’re celebrating Diwali or not — or even know what it is — it’s an absolute star, unique without being bizarre, engaging through and through.

81.6 proof.

A / $220 [BUY IT NOW FROM FROOTBAT]
